tips.title: Four changes, two temperatures
tips.body: **Melting and freezing** both happen at the **melting point**; **boiling and condensing** both at the **boiling point**. There is no separate freezing point, and a data table will be labelled *melting point* either way.

tips.title: Melting does not break covalent bonds
tips.body: It overcomes the forces **between** the molecules. The bonds **inside** each molecule survive — which is why steam is still H₂O. This is the commonest error in chemistry at this level.

tips.title: The specification names three limitations
tips.body: **No forces** in the model; all particles shown as **spheres**; the spheres are **solid**. A question asking for *limitations* expects more than one, and the first is the one worth explaining.

tips.title: (l) is not (aq)
tips.body: **(l)** is a **pure liquid** — NaCl(l) is molten salt. **(aq)** is **dissolved in water** — NaCl(aq) is salt solution. They give different products in electrolysis, so the symbol carries real information.

tips.title: Evaporation is not boiling
tips.body: **Evaporation** happens at **any** temperature and only at the **surface**. **Boiling** happens at the **boiling point** and throughout the liquid. A puddle drying on a cold day is evaporating.

steps.title: The three states, and the four changes
steps.body:
The three states of matter are **solid**, **liquid** and **gas**.

There are **four** changes between them, and they happen at **two** temperatures:

- **Melting** — solid to liquid — at the **melting point**
- **Freezing** — liquid to solid — at the **melting point**
- **Boiling** — liquid to gas — at the **boiling point**
- **Condensing** — gas to liquid — at the **boiling point**

**Notice that each temperature governs two changes**, one in each direction. Water melts at 0 °C and freezes at 0 °C — the same temperature, because it is the same boundary crossed in opposite directions. There is no separate *freezing point*; the spec calls it the **melting point** either way.

That is worth getting right, because a question asking *at what temperature does this substance freeze?* is answered by its **melting point**, and the data table will be labelled that way.

**A caution about boiling.** Evaporation also turns liquid into gas, but it happens at **any** temperature and only from the **surface**. **Boiling** happens at the **boiling point** and throughout the liquid. Both are liquid to gas, but they are not the same process.

steps.title: The simple particle model
steps.body:
**The three states can be represented by a simple model.** In this model, **particles are represented by small solid spheres**.

**Particle theory can help to explain melting, boiling, freezing and condensing**, and the explanation is always about **arrangement and movement**:

- **Solid** — particles packed closely in a **regular** arrangement, **vibrating** about fixed positions. Fixed shape and fixed volume.
- **Liquid** — particles close together but **irregularly** arranged and able to **move past each other**. Fixed volume, but takes the shape of its container.
- **Gas** — particles far apart, moving **quickly and randomly** in all directions. No fixed shape and no fixed volume.

**Heating gives the particles more energy.** They vibrate or move faster, and at the melting or boiling point they have enough energy to **overcome the forces holding them in place**. Cooling does the reverse.

**The energy needed to change state depends on the strength of the forces between the particles.** That is the sentence to learn, because it links this topic to bonding: a substance with strong forces between its particles needs a lot of energy to separate them.

**And what those particles are depends on the substance.** The spec puts it precisely: *the nature of the particles involved depends on the type of bonding and the structure of the substance.* In sodium chloride the particles are **ions**; in water they are **molecules**; in a metal they are **atoms** in a lattice of positive ions. The word *particle* is deliberately vague, and being able to say what the particles actually are in a given substance is a Higher-tier move.

steps.title: Stronger forces mean higher melting and boiling points
steps.body:
**This part is Higher tier.**

$$\textbf{the stronger the forces between the particles, the higher the melting and boiling points}$$

The reasoning is short and you should be able to give it: changing state means **separating the particles**, or at least letting them move past each other. Stronger forces need **more energy** to overcome, and more energy means a **higher temperature**.

**This explains the whole pattern you will meet in bonding:**

- **Small molecules** — like water or carbon dioxide — have **weak forces between the molecules**, so low melting and boiling points. Many are gases or liquids at room temperature.
- **Ionic compounds** — like sodium chloride — have **strong electrostatic forces in all directions** between oppositely charged ions, so high melting and boiling points.
- **Giant covalent structures** — like diamond — have **strong covalent bonds** throughout, so very high melting points.
- **Metals** have strong forces between the positive ions and the delocalised electrons, so generally high melting points.

**The mistake to avoid** is saying that melting a molecular substance breaks the covalent bonds. It does not. Melting and boiling overcome the **forces between** the molecules; the bonds **inside** each molecule stay intact. That distinction — **between** molecules against **inside** them — decides several marks in the bonding topics, and it starts here.

steps.title: Where the model stops working
steps.body:
The simple model is useful, but the spec asks you to know its **limitations** — and it names **exactly three**. Learn all three, because a question asking for *limitations*, plural, expects more than one.

1. **In the model there are no forces between the particles.** This is the most serious limitation, because the forces are precisely what decides melting and boiling points. The model that explains changes of state leaves out the thing that causes them.
2. **All particles are represented as spheres.** Real particles are not spheres. Molecules have shapes — water is bent, carbon dioxide is linear — and those shapes affect how the substance behaves.
3. **The spheres are solid.** Real atoms are mostly **empty space**, with a tiny dense nucleus and electrons occupying the volume around it. A solid sphere is the opposite of what an atom is like.

**Why this matters more than it looks.** Every scientific model is a simplification, and knowing where a model stops is part of using it properly. The particle model predicts changes of state well and tells you nothing at all about why a particular substance melts at a particular temperature — for that you need bonding.

**In an answer**, name the limitation and say **what it costs you**: *the model shows no forces between particles, yet the strength of those forces is what determines the melting point, so the model cannot explain why substances differ.*

steps.title: State symbols
steps.body:
In chemical equations the state of each substance is shown by a **state symbol** written in brackets after the formula.


**In use:**

- $\mathrm{CaCO_3(s) \rightarrow CaO(s) + CO_2(g)}$
- $\mathrm{HCl(aq) + NaOH(aq) \rightarrow NaCl(aq) + H_2O(l)}$
- $\mathrm{Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) \rightarrow MgCl_2(aq) + H_2(g)}$

**The one to be careful with is (l) against (aq).**

- **(l)** means the substance is a **pure liquid** — water on its own is $\mathrm{H_2O(l)}$.
- **(aq)** means it is **dissolved in water** — salt water is $\mathrm{NaCl(aq)}$, not $\mathrm{NaCl(l)}$.

Molten sodium chloride, heated until it melts, **is** $\mathrm{NaCl(l)}$ — and that is a genuinely different substance from salt solution, as the electrolysis topics show. Getting this symbol wrong changes what you have claimed.

**You are expected to include state symbols** in equations for the reactions in the specification, so add them as a habit rather than only when asked.

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**Melting and freezing share a temperature, and so do boiling and condensing.** There is no separate freezing point — a data table gives a **melting point**, and a substance freezes at it. Four changes, two temperatures.

**Say what the particles actually are.** The spec is careful: *the nature of the particles involved depends on the type of bonding and the structure of the substance.* In sodium chloride they are **ions**; in water, **molecules**; in a metal, **positive ions** in a sea of delocalised electrons. Writing *particles* throughout is safe; naming them correctly is better, and in a bonding question it is the difference between a general answer and a specific one.

**Melting a molecular substance does not break covalent bonds.** It overcomes the **forces between** the molecules. The bonds **inside** each molecule survive — which is why steam is still $\mathrm{H_2O}$. This single distinction decides several marks across the bonding topics, and it is the commonest error in the whole of chemistry at this level.

**Know all three limitations, and what each one costs.** The strongest answer is about the first: the model shows **no forces**, yet the **strength of the forces is what determines the melting point**. So the model can describe *that* a substance melts and can never explain *why this one melts at 801 °C and that one at 0 °C. For that you need bonding — which is exactly why states of matter is taught before bonding and revisited inside it.

**(l) and (aq) are not interchangeable.** $\mathrm{NaCl(l)}$ is molten salt — heated past its melting point. $\mathrm{NaCl(aq)}$ is salt dissolved in water. They behave completely differently in electrolysis, giving different products, so the symbol is carrying real information rather than decorating the equation.

**Evaporation is not boiling.** Both take liquid to gas. **Evaporation** happens at **any** temperature and only at the **surface**; **boiling** happens at the **boiling point** and throughout the liquid. A question about a puddle drying on a cold day is about evaporation, and answering it with *the water boiled* is wrong.

**Every model has a boundary, and knowing it is part of knowing the model.** That is a genuinely scientific idea, and questions about limitations are testing whether you hold it — not whether you can criticise a diagram.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- The three states are **solid**, **liquid** and **gas**.
- **Melting** and **freezing** happen at the **melting point**; **boiling** and **condensing** at the **boiling point**.
- Four changes, **two** temperatures — there is no separate freezing point.
- In the simple model, **particles are represented by small solid spheres**.
- **Solid**: close, regular, vibrating in place. **Liquid**: close, irregular, moving past each other. **Gas**: far apart, fast and random.
- The energy needed to change state depends on the **strength of the forces between the particles**.
- What the particles are depends on the **bonding and structure**: ions, molecules or atoms.
- **(HT)** The **stronger the forces, the higher the melting and boiling points.**
- Melting a molecular substance overcomes the forces **between** molecules; the covalent bonds **inside** them do not break.
- The model's **three limitations**: there are **no forces** in it; all particles are shown as **spheres**; the spheres are **solid**.
- The first limitation is why the model cannot explain **why** substances differ in melting point.
- State symbols: **(s)** solid, **(l)** liquid, **(g)** gas, **(aq)** dissolved in water.
- **(l)** is a pure liquid; **(aq)** is a solution — and they behave differently.
- **Evaporation** happens at any temperature, from the surface; **boiling** at the boiling point, throughout.

questions.prompt: Describe the arrangement and movement of particles in each of the three states of matter, and explain what happens to them when a solid is heated until it boils.
questions.solution: In a solid the particles are packed closely together in a regular arrangement and vibrate about fixed positions, which is why a solid has both a fixed shape and a fixed volume. In a liquid the particles are still close together but their arrangement is irregular, and they are able to move past one another, so a liquid has a fixed volume but takes the shape of its container. In a gas the particles are far apart and move quickly and randomly in all directions, so a gas has neither a fixed shape nor a fixed volume. When a solid is heated, energy is transferred to its particles and they vibrate more vigorously about their fixed positions. At the melting point the particles have gained enough energy to overcome the forces holding them in their fixed positions, so the regular arrangement breaks down and the particles become able to move past one another. The solid melts and becomes a liquid. Continued heating gives the particles still more energy and they move faster. At the boiling point the particles have enough energy to overcome the forces between them completely and escape from the liquid, so the liquid boils and becomes a gas. Throughout this process the amount of energy required depends on the strength of the forces between the particles, so a substance with strong forces has a high melting point and a high boiling point. It is important to note that in a molecular substance it is the forces between the molecules that are overcome and not the covalent bonds within them, which remain intact.

questions.modelAnswer:
**The three states:**

| State | Arrangement | Movement | Shape and volume |
|---|---|---|---|
| solid | close, **regular** | vibrating about **fixed positions** | fixed shape, fixed volume |
| liquid | close, **irregular** | moving **past each other** | container's shape, fixed volume |
| gas | **far apart** | fast and random | neither fixed |

**Heating a solid:**

1. Energy is transferred to the particles and they **vibrate more vigorously**.
2. At the **melting point** they have enough energy to **overcome the forces holding them in fixed positions** — the regular arrangement breaks down and they can move past one another. It **melts**.
3. Further heating makes them move faster still.
4. At the **boiling point** they can **overcome the forces between them completely and escape** the liquid. It **boils**.

**The mark that lifts the answer:** the energy needed depends on the **strength of the forces between the particles** — and in a molecular substance it is the forces **between** molecules that are overcome, **not** the covalent bonds within them.

questions.prompt: Give the limitations of the simple particle model, and explain why they matter.
questions.solution: The specification names three limitations of the simple model in which particles are represented by small solid spheres. The first is that in the model there are no forces between the particles. The second is that all particles are represented as spheres. The third is that the spheres are solid. The first of these is the most serious, because the strength of the forces between particles is exactly what determines the melting point and the boiling point of a substance. The model can therefore describe what happens when a substance changes state, but it cannot explain why sodium chloride melts at a far higher temperature than water does, since the very feature responsible for that difference is absent from the model. To explain that, knowledge of bonding and structure is needed. The second limitation matters because real particles are not spherical. Molecules have definite shapes, for example a water molecule is bent and a carbon dioxide molecule is linear, and these shapes affect how the substances behave. The third matters because real atoms are mostly empty space, consisting of a very small dense nucleus with electrons occupying the volume around it, so a solid sphere is close to the opposite of what an atom actually is. More generally, every scientific model is a simplification, and knowing where a model stops working is part of using it properly rather than a criticism of it.

criteria.text: Explains why the absence of forces matters

questions.modelAnswer:
**The three limitations the specification names:**

1. **There are no forces between the particles** in the model.
2. **All particles are represented as spheres.**
3. **The spheres are solid.**

**Why the first matters most.** The **strength of the forces** between particles is exactly what determines the melting and boiling points. So the model can describe *that* a substance changes state, but can never explain **why sodium chloride melts far above water** — the very feature responsible is absent. For that you need **bonding and structure**.

**Why the second matters.** Real particles are not spherical. **Water is bent, carbon dioxide is linear**, and those shapes affect behaviour.

**Why the third matters.** Real atoms are **mostly empty space** — a tiny dense nucleus with electrons around it. A solid sphere is close to the opposite.

**And the general point worth finishing on:** every scientific model is a simplification, and knowing where one stops working is part of **using** it properly, not a criticism of it.

examTechnique.body:
Give the melting point as the temperature of both melting and freezing.

Describe both the arrangement and the movement of the particles when asked about a state.

Say that melting and boiling overcome the forces between particles, not the bonds within molecules.

Give all three limitations when a question asks for limitations of the model.

Explain why a limitation matters, not just what it is.

Include state symbols in every equation, and distinguish a pure liquid from a solution.

Name what the particles actually are when the substance is known: ions, molecules or atoms.
examinerErrors: Treating the freezing point as a different temperature from the melting point.
Writing that melting breaks covalent bonds.
Giving only one limitation of the particle model.
Using (l) for a substance dissolved in water.
Describing arrangement but not movement, or the reverse.
Saying the particles are always atoms.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer explains changes of state in terms of the forces between particles rather than the particles themselves, and never confuses those forces with the bonds inside a molecule. It names all three limitations of the model and explains the first properly: the model has no forces, and the forces are what set the melting point, so the model can describe melting and can never explain why one substance melts far above another. It says what the particles actually are in a named substance, and it treats a state symbol as information rather than decoration.
